question: An OTDR trace shows a step loss of 0.4 dB at a splice location with no accompanying reflection, and a nearby splice tray was recently reworked. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: A poor-quality fusion splice or a macrobend from tight fiber coiling in the reworked tray
A connector that was left unmated
Normal cable attenuation for that distance
An OTDR wavelength mismatch

explanation: 0.4 dB is well above the acceptable splice loss target (~0.10 dB) and shows no Fresnel reflection, pointing to either a marginal splice or a macrobend introduced when the tray was reworked.

question: A tech arrives at a manhole and the four-gas meter reads 18.2% oxygen. What should happen next?

choices.text: Do not enter — the atmosphere is oxygen-deficient; ventilate and retest before considering entry
Enter quickly since 18.2% is close to the 19.5% threshold
Enter with a self-contained breathing apparatus and proceed as normal
Retest only if a strange odor is present

category: The Telecom Industry and OSP Career
explanation: 18.2% is below the 19.5% oxygen-deficient threshold. No entry is permitted until the space is ventilated and retests within the safe 19.5–23.5% range.

question: A structured cabling certification report shows a NEXT failure at the patch panel end of a Cat 6 link, with insertion loss and return loss both passing comfortably. What should the tech check first?

choices.text: Whether the pairs were untwisted more than 6mm during termination at the patch panel
Whether the cable run exceeds 90 meters
Whether the wrong category cable was pulled
Whether the certification tester needs recalibration

explanation: A NEXT-only failure with passing IL and RL points to a termination issue, not a cable or length problem. Excessive untwisting at the patch panel (beyond 6mm for Cat 6) is the classic cause.

question: A cell site loses utility power. The tech observes the site never went dark and baseband equipment shows no interruption. Six hours later, an LVD event drops non-critical lighting loads. What does this sequence indicate?

choices.text: The system worked exactly as designed — batteries floated seamlessly through the outage and LVD correctly shed non-critical load as the battery approached its discharge limit
A rectifier failure caused the delayed LVD event
The generator failed to start, which is why LVD activated
This sequence indicates a wiring fault requiring immediate site shutdown

explanation: No interruption at utility loss confirms the batteries floated seamlessly onto the bus. The LVD event six hours later is the expected load-shedding behavior as the battery approaches its low-voltage threshold — not a fault.

question: A splicer measures a completed splice at 0.03 dB from one end but 0.28 dB from the opposite end on a bidirectional OTDR test. What is the correct accepted splice loss?

choices.text: The average of both directions: approximately 0.155 dB
Always the lower of the two readings
Always the higher of the two readings, to be conservative
Whichever reading was taken first

explanation: TIA-526-7 requires the accepted splice loss to be the average of both directional measurements, since fiber geometry at the interface makes single-direction readings directionally biased.

question: A DSL loop qualification test shows excessive noise and an unexpected impedance change partway down a copper pair. What tool would a tech use next to locate the physical cause?

choices.text: A TDR, to locate the distance to the impedance change
An OTDR, since copper and fiber use the same test equipment
A fiber inspection probe
A four-gas meter

explanation: A TDR is the copper-plant equivalent of an OTDR — it sends a pulse down the conductor and calculates the distance to any impedance change such as a bridged tap, water intrusion, or splice fault.

question: A fiber link's OLTS measurement shows 9.5 dB of loss against a calculated budget of 22 dB. Certification should be marked as:

choices.text: Passing, with a healthy 12.5 dB margin
Failing, since any measured loss above zero is unacceptable
Inconclusive without an OTDR trace
Failing, since 9.5 dB exceeds the connector loss limit alone

explanation: Margin = 22 dB budget − 9.5 dB measured loss = 12.5 dB positive margin. A link with positive margin passes; an OTDR trace is useful for locating problems, not required to declare pass/fail on an OLTS reading.

question: A tech is asked to terminate pairs onto an existing 66-block in a central office that also has newer 110-blocks nearby. Which tool should be used on the 66-block?

choices.text: A 66-type punchdown tool, matched to that block's IDC geometry
Whichever tool is closest at hand, since both blocks accept the same tool
A 110-type tool, since it is the newer standard
No tool is needed — 66-blocks use screw terminals

explanation: Tool selection must match the specific block type present, not the newest available tool. A 110-type tool used on a 66-block damages the terminals.

question: A closeout package for a completed 48-strand fiber build is missing OTDR traces for 6 of the splices. What should happen before the job is considered complete?

choices.text: The missing splices should be re-tested and their traces added before submitting the closeout package
The job can close out with a note explaining the gap
Missing traces only matter if the customer specifically requests them
OTDR traces are optional for splices under 0.10 dB

explanation: Every splice needs a verifying trace as part of the permanent record. An incomplete package risks warranty issues and leaves future techs without a baseline for those specific splices.

question: While climbing a shared utility pole, a tech notices a power line closer than the minimum approach distance allows. The correct action is to:

choices.text: Descend and call the utility before proceeding — do not attempt the work
Continue climbing but avoid touching anything metal
Proceed if wearing insulated gloves rated for low voltage
Reroute the telecom cable path without utility involvement

category: The Telecom Industry and OSP Career
explanation: Telecom techs do not work on or near energized power lines when minimum approach distance can't be maintained. The utility must be contacted to de-energize or provide safety coverage.

question: A cell site's battery string passed its monthly float voltage check but failed the quarterly impedance test with a rising trend over the last three quarters. What does this indicate?

choices.text: The battery string is weakening internally even though it still floats normally — it should be scheduled for replacement before it fails during an outage
Nothing — impedance testing is not a meaningful indicator of battery health
The rectifiers are undersized
The LVD threshold needs to be lowered

explanation: Float voltage can look normal while internal impedance rises, an early warning sign of cell degradation. Trending impedance data catches weakening batteries before they fail silently during a real outage.

question: A fiber inspection probe shows contamination confined entirely to Zone D (the ferrule) with a perfectly clean Zone A. What is the practical impact on the connection?

choices.text: Minimal — Zone D contamination outside the optical path is far less critical than contamination in Zone A
The connector cannot be used under any circumstances
It causes the same insertion loss as Zone A contamination
It requires replacing the entire cable

explanation: IEC 61300-3-35 allows more contamination tolerance in Zone D since it's outside the direct optical path, unlike Zone A (the core) where even tiny defects cause significant loss.

question: A DMARC extension is being run from an exterior NID to an MDF two floors up, passing through an air-handling plenum space on one floor. What cable rating is required in the plenum section?

choices.text: CMP (plenum-rated) for that section, even if CMR is used elsewhere in the run
CMR is acceptable everywhere, including plenum spaces
Standard CM cable is fine as long as the run is short
No specific rating applies to DMARC extensions

explanation: Fire code rating requirements apply per space, not per whole run — any segment passing through an air-handling plenum must use CMP-rated cable regardless of what's used elsewhere.

question: An OTDR trace of a newly spliced 12 km link shows a consistent, linear slope with a step loss at 6 km and a large reflective spike at the very end. How should this trace be read?

choices.text: Normal cable attenuation, a mid-span splice at 6 km, and a connector or open end-face at the far end
A break at 6 km and a splice at the far end
The entire trace indicates a failed link requiring immediate re-splice
A macrobend at 6 km and a fusion splice at the far end

explanation: A step loss without reflection at 6 km is consistent with a fusion splice; the large reflective spike at the end is the signature of a connector or unterminated fiber end-face — a normal, healthy trace.

question: A generator exerciser log shows the cell site generator has not run its scheduled weekly cycle in five weeks due to a controller fault. What is the primary operational risk?

choices.text: An undetected mechanical or fuel-system failure could go unnoticed until a real utility outage demands the generator
No risk — exercising is a purely cosmetic maintenance task
The battery string automatically compensates for a non-exercised generator indefinitely
The ATS will refuse to transfer load if the generator hasn't exercised recently

explanation: Regular exercising is what surfaces fuel, starting, and mechanical problems before they matter. A five-week gap means any developing fault has gone undetected — exactly the scenario exercising is meant to prevent.
